Common expressions from fans: 'Come on!' / 'Let's go!' / 'What a goal!' / 'Offside!' / 'That's a foul!'
'Could I get a beer / hot dog / nachos from the stand, please?'
content.tip: In the UK, football fans say 'match' — not 'game'. In the USA, 'game' is used for everything. English stadiums are called 'grounds', American ones are 'stadiums' or 'arenas'.

content.subtitle: Museums, Tours & Cultural Sites
content.explanation: These phrases will help you get the most out of cultural experiences abroad.
examples: 'Is there an audio guide available? In English, please.'
'How much is the entrance fee?' / 'Is entry free?'
'Are there guided tours? How long do they last?'
'Is photography allowed inside?'
'Could you take a photo of us, please?' / 'Would you mind taking a picture of me with this?'
'Could you point me to the gift shop / café / exit?'
'Excuse me, where is the [specific exhibit / gallery / artwork]?'
'What are your opening hours?' / 'What time do you close today?'
content.tip: Many major museums in cities like London (British Museum, Tate Modern, Natural History Museum) and New York (MoMA, Metropolitan Museum) offer free entry or pay-what-you-wish admission. Always check the website in advance.

content.subtitle: At the Supermarket
content.explanation: Supermarkets in English-speaking countries have their own vocabulary and social norms. These phrases cover everything from finding products to checking out.
examples: 'Excuse me, where can I find the [dairy products / bread aisle / frozen foods]?'
'Is this on offer / on sale?' / 'Is there a buy-one-get-one-free deal on this?'
'Do you have a loyalty card?' / 'I don't have one — can I sign up?'
'Could I get a bag, please?' / 'I have my own bag.' (reusable bags are common)
'I think I was charged twice for this item — could you check?'
'Could I pay by card?' / 'Do you accept contactless?' / 'Is Apple Pay accepted?'
Self-checkout: 'Unexpected item in the bagging area' — this is a common machine error! Ask staff for help.
Common labels: 'Best before' (quality date) | 'Use by' (safety date — do not eat after this) | 'Sell by' (for store use)
content.tip: 'Aisle' is pronounced 'EYE-ul' — not 'ay-zel'. UK supermarkets use 'trolley' (US: cart) and 'queue' (US: line). In the US, the cashier may ask 'Paper or plastic?' meaning which type of bag you want.

content.subtitle: Clothes & Electronics Stores
content.explanation: From asking for your size to negotiating a return, these phrases cover the full shopping experience.
examples: 'I'm just browsing, thank you.' (when you don't need help)
'Could I try this on, please?' / 'Where are the fitting rooms / changing rooms?'
'Do you have this in a size medium / large?' / 'Do you have this in a different colour?'
'This is slightly too big / small / tight. Do you have the next size up / down?'
'How much is this?' / 'Is this the final price?' / 'Is there a discount available?'
'Could I pay in instalments?' (for expensive electronics)
'I'd like to return this, please. I have the receipt.' / 'I'd like to exchange it for a different size.'
'Is this covered by a warranty?' / 'What is your returns policy?'
content.tip: UK clothing sizes differ from US, European, and Brazilian sizes. Always try items on or check a size conversion chart. When returning items, most stores require the original receipt and packaging, and some have a 28-30 day return window.

content.subtitle: Street Markets & Bargaining
content.explanation: In some markets (flea markets, tourist markets), bargaining is expected. In others (UK, US, Australia), prices are fixed. Know the difference!
examples: 'How much is this?' / 'What's the best price you can do for this?'
'That's a bit more than I was hoping to spend. Could you do [lower price]?'
'I'll take two — could you give me a discount?'
'Is this handmade / locally produced?' / 'What material is this made from?'
'I'll think about it and come back.' (polite way to leave without buying)
'Do you take cards here, or is it cash only?'
'Could you wrap this for me? It's a gift.'
Expressions sellers use: 'Best quality!' / 'Special price for you!' / 'Last one!' / 'My friend, come look!'
content.tip: Bargaining is common in markets in Morocco, Turkey, Southeast Asia, and parts of Latin America. In the USA, UK, and Australia, fixed prices are the norm — bargaining at chain stores will be met with confusion. Street markets and flea markets are exceptions.

content.subtitle: Meeting People & Small Talk
content.explanation: Travelling is one of the best ways to practise real English conversation. These phrases help you make connections with locals and fellow travellers.
examples: 'Hi! I'm [name]. I'm from Brazil — have you been there?'
'Is this your first time in [city]? Any recommendations?'
'Where are you from? / How long have you been here?'
'What do you do back home? / Are you travelling alone or with family?'
'Could you recommend a good local restaurant — not too touristy?'
'This weather is incredible / terrible, isn't it?' (classic British opener!)
'I love your city — the [food / architecture / people] is amazing.'
'Could I add you on Instagram? / Can we swap numbers?'
content.tip: Small talk is a genuine social skill in English-speaking cultures — especially in the UK, USA, Canada, and Australia. Topics like weather, sports, and weekend plans are always safe. Avoid asking about salary, weight, or age with people you've just met.

content.subtitle: Asking for Help & Directions
content.explanation: Never be afraid to ask for help — locals generally appreciate polite tourists who make an effort.
examples: 'Excuse me, could you help me? I'm a bit lost.'
'How do I get to [place] from here? Is it within walking distance?'
'Is it far? / Roughly how long does it take on foot?'
Directions you'll hear: 'Turn left / right at the traffic lights.' | 'Go straight ahead for two blocks.' | 'It's just around the corner.' | 'You can't miss it.'
'Sorry, could you repeat that more slowly, please? My English is still improving.'
'Could you write that down / show me on my phone map?'
'Is there a pharmacy / hospital / police station nearby?'
'I need help — please call the police / an ambulance / the fire brigade.'
content.tip: Use Google Maps offline mode before exploring — download the city map when you have Wi-Fi so it works without data. And don't be embarrassed to ask locals twice — it's a sign of confidence, not weakness!

content.subtitle: Useful Expressions for Every Situation
content.explanation: A toolkit of versatile phrases that will get you through almost any situation abroad.
examples: Polite requests: 'Could you...?' / 'Would it be possible to...?' / 'I was wondering if...'
Showing you didn't understand: 'I'm sorry, I didn't quite catch that.' / 'Could you say that again?' / 'I'm not sure I follow — could you explain?'
Buying time to think: 'Let me see...' / 'Good question — I think...' / 'If I understand correctly...'
Showing appreciation: 'That's really helpful, thank you so much.' / 'I really appreciate it.' / 'You've been incredibly kind.'
Excusing yourself: 'Excuse me.' / 'I beg your pardon.' / 'Sorry to interrupt, but...'
Handling confusion: 'I think there may have been a misunderstanding.' / 'Let me clarify...'
Emergencies: 'Help!' / 'Call 999 (UK) / 911 (USA) / 112 (EU)!' / 'I need a doctor!' / 'I've been robbed!'
content.tip: The single most useful phrase when travelling: 'I'm sorry, my English isn't perfect — could you speak a little more slowly?' Native speakers will always accommodate you, and making the effort to speak English is always appreciated.

quiz.title: Travel English Challenge
quiz.description: Test your travel vocabulary and phrases for real-world situations abroad

questions.question: At the airport check-in desk, what does 'carry-on luggage' mean?
options: Luggage that is checked in and goes in the cargo hold
A small bag you take with you onto the plane
Luggage that is too heavy and requires an extra fee
Fragile items that need special handling
questions.explanation: 'Carry-on' (also called 'hand luggage' in British English) is the small bag you bring inside the cabin with you. Most airlines allow one carry-on bag and one personal item (handbag or laptop bag). Size and weight limits vary by airline.

questions.question: An immigration officer asks: 'Do you have anything to declare?' The correct response if you have nothing is:
questions.explanation: 'Nothing to declare' is the standard phrase at customs. If you ARE carrying cash over the limit (usually USD/GBP 10,000), restricted foods, or taxable goods above the duty-free allowance, you must declare them honestly — failing to do so is a serious offence.

questions.question: At a restaurant in the USA, the waiter says 'How is everything?' This means:
options: They want you to pay the bill now
They are asking if you are enjoying your food and if you need anything
They are asking about your travel plans
They are apologising for a delay
questions.explanation: In American restaurants, waiters check in regularly during the meal. 'How is everything?' = 'Are you enjoying your food? Do you need anything?' The polite response is 'Wonderful, thank you!' or 'Actually, could I get a bit more water?'

questions.question: In British English, 'the bill' at a restaurant is called what in American English?
questions.explanation: In American English, you ask for 'the check' when you want to pay. In British English, you ask for 'the bill'. 'Tab' is informal in both, often used in bars. 'Receipt' is the paper you receive AFTER paying.

questions.question: On the London Underground, the announcement says 'Mind the gap.' This means:
options: Be careful of the space between the train and the platform edge
questions.explanation: 'Mind the gap' is one of the most iconic phrases in British public transport. It warns passengers to be careful of the gap between the train carriage and the platform edge, which can be large enough to trip or fall into, especially on curved platforms.

questions.question: You're in a clothes store and want to try on a jacket. What do you say?
questions.explanation: 'Try on' is the correct phrasal verb for trying on clothes. 'Could I try this on?' is polite and natural. You might also ask 'Where are the fitting rooms / changing rooms?' The word 'fitting room' is used in both British and American English.

questions.question: You want to ask a local for directions. Which is the most polite and natural opener?
options: 'Tell me how to get to the museum.'
'Excuse me, could you help me? I'm trying to find the museum.'
questions.explanation: Starting with 'Excuse me' gets someone's attention politely. 'Could you help me?' is a soft, indirect request. This combination is natural, polite, and very commonly used by native speakers when approaching strangers for directions.

questions.question: A shop assistant says 'I'm just browsing, thanks.' This means:
options: You said this to indicate you don't need help yet
You want to buy something immediately
questions.explanation: 'I'm just browsing' is what YOU say to the shop assistant when they offer help and you don't need it yet. It means 'I'm just looking around — I don't need assistance at this moment.' It's a very common, polite way to decline help without being rude.

questions.question: What emergency number should you call in the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: In the UK, the emergency number is 999 (police, fire, ambulance). In the USA and Canada, it is 911. In most of Europe, it is 112. In Australia, it is 000. Note: 112 also works in the UK and most countries as a universal emergency number.

questions.question: A food label says 'Use by 20 March.' This means:
options: The food tastes best before that date but is still safe after
The food must not be eaten after that date for safety reasons
The store must sell it before that date
The food was produced on that date
questions.explanation: 'Use by' is a safety date — do NOT consume the product after this date, as it may be unsafe. This is different from 'Best before', which is a quality date — the food may still be safe to eat after a 'best before' date but may have lost quality. 'Sell by' is for store inventory management only.

sections.title: Career & Job Opportunities
sections.description: Resumes, interviews, LinkedIn, and professional communication for international careers

content.subtitle: Power Verbs for Achievements
content.explanation: Start every bullet point with a strong action verb instead of weak phrases like 'was responsible for'. Recruiters scan resumes in seconds, so verbs need to show impact immediately.
examples: Led a team of 5 developers to deliver the project two weeks early.
Increased website conversion rate by 18% through UX redesign.
Streamlined the onboarding process, reducing training time by 30%.
Implemented a new CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions.
Negotiated contracts with three international suppliers.
content.tip: Avoid 'responsible for' and 'worked on'. Use: led, built, launched, increased, reduced, negotiated, designed, automated.

content.subtitle: Quantifying Your Impact
content.explanation: Numbers make achievements concrete and credible. Whenever possible, add a metric: percentage, amount of money, number of people, or time saved.
examples: Reduced page load time from 4s to 1.2s, improving user retention by 12%.
Managed a budget of $50,000 for the marketing campaign.
Trained 15 new employees during the company's expansion.
Handled an average of 40 client tickets per week with a 95% satisfaction rate.
content.tip: If you don't have exact numbers, use reasonable estimates: 'approximately', 'over', 'more than'.

content.subtitle: Resume Structure & Key Sections
content.explanation: An international resume usually follows this order: Contact Info → Professional Summary → Work Experience → Skills → Education → Certifications/Projects.
examples: Professional Summary: 'Front-end developer with 2+ years of experience building responsive web applications with React and Angular.'
Skills section: 'Technical Skills: JavaScript, TypeScript, React, Node.js, PostgreSQL, Git.'
Education: 'B.Sc. in Computer Science, Federal Rural University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRRJ), 2023.'
content.tip: Keep it to one page if you have less than 10 years of experience. Tailor the summary for each job application.

content.subtitle: Cover Letter Opening & Closing
content.explanation: A strong opening states the position and shows genuine interest. The closing should restate your value and include a clear call to action.
examples: I am writing to apply for the Front-End Developer position advertised on LinkedIn.
With two years of experience in React and Angular, I am confident I can contribute to your team from day one.
I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my background aligns with your needs.
Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to hearing from you.
content.tip: Never start with 'My name is...'. Start with the position and your value proposition instead.

content.subtitle: LinkedIn Profile & Networking Messages
content.explanation: Your LinkedIn headline should describe what you do and the value you bring, not just your job title. Networking messages should be short, specific, and polite.
examples: Headline: 'Full-Stack Developer | React, Node.js, Java | Open to Opportunities'
Connection request: 'Hi Sarah, I really enjoyed your talk on scalable APIs. I'd love to connect and follow your work.'
Cold outreach: 'Hi John, I noticed your team is hiring a Junior Developer. I have experience with Angular and Firebase and would love to learn more about the role.'
About section opener: 'I'm a developer passionate about building fast, accessible web applications.'
content.tip: Keep networking messages under 300 characters — busy professionals rarely reply to long messages from strangers.

content.subtitle: Following Up After Applying
content.explanation: A polite follow-up shows initiative without being pushy. Wait about one week after applying or after an interview before reaching out.
examples: I wanted to follow up on my application for the Developer position submitted last week.
I remain very interested in the role and would appreciate any update on the hiring process.
Thank you again for the interview on Tuesday — I really enjoyed learning more about the team.
Please let me know if you need any additional information from my side.
content.tip: One follow-up is professional; more than two can seem impatient. Always keep the tone warm and respectful.

content.subtitle: Answering Common Interview Questions
content.explanation: Interviewers ask predictable opening questions. Prepare concise, confident answers that connect your background to the role.
examples: 'Tell me about yourself.' → 'I'm a front-end developer with two years of experience, currently focused on React and TypeScript. I'm particularly interested in building accessible, high-performance interfaces.'
'Why do you want to work here?' → 'I admire how your team combines strong engineering practices with real user impact, and I'd love to contribute to that.'
'What is your biggest weakness?' → 'I used to spend too much time perfecting small details, so I've learned to set clear time limits for each task.'
'Where do you see yourself in five years?' → 'I see myself growing into a senior developer role, mentoring junior engineers along the way.'
content.tip: Keep answers between 30-90 seconds. Practice out loud — silence and hesitation hurt more than small grammar mistakes.

content.subtitle: Behavioral Questions — The STAR Method
content.explanation: Behavioral questions ask about past experiences. Structure your answer using STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
examples: Situation: 'In my last project, we were close to missing a delivery deadline.'
Task: 'I was responsible for the front-end integration with the API.'
Action: 'I reorganized my priorities and worked closely with the back-end team to fix blocking issues.'
Result: 'We delivered the project on time and the client praised the app's performance.'
content.tip: Common triggers for STAR questions: 'Tell me about a time when...', 'Describe a situation where...', 'Give me an example of...'

content.subtitle: Questions to Ask the Interviewer
content.explanation: Asking thoughtful questions shows genuine interest and helps you evaluate the company too.
examples: What does success look like in this role after the first six months?
Can you tell me more about the team I'd be working with?
What are the biggest challenges the team is currently facing?
What opportunities are there for professional growth or learning?
What are the next steps in the hiring process?
content.tip: Never say 'I don't have any questions' — it can suggest a lack of interest in the role.

content.subtitle: Salary Negotiation Phrases
content.explanation: Negotiating salary in English requires confident but polite language, focused on value rather than personal need.
examples: Based on my research and experience, I was expecting a range closer to $X.
Is there any flexibility in the base salary for this position?
I'm very excited about this opportunity — could we discuss the compensation package in more detail?
Besides salary, could you tell me more about benefits like remote work or professional development budget?
content.tip: Always let the employer mention a number first if possible, and never apologize for negotiating.

content.subtitle: Professional Email Etiquette
content.explanation: Workplace emails should be clear, polite, and structured: greeting, purpose, details, and a clear closing.
examples: Subject: 'Follow-up: Sprint Planning Meeting Notes'
Hi team, I hope you're all doing well. I wanted to share a quick update on the project.
Could you please review the attached document and share your feedback by Friday?
Let me know if you have any questions — happy to jump on a call.
Best regards, / Thanks in advance,
content.tip: CC only people who truly need the information; BCC is used for privacy in mass emails, not for internal team threads.

content.subtitle: Remote Work & Freelance Vocabulary
content.explanation: Remote and freelance work has its own vocabulary that's essential for international, distributed teams.
examples: Async communication: updates shared without expecting an immediate reply.
Standup meeting: a short daily check-in about progress and blockers.
Time zone overlap: hours when both teams are online at the same time.
Deliverable: a specific output you agreed to produce, e.g., 'the deliverable is due next Monday.'
Scope creep: when a project's requirements keep expanding beyond the original agreement.
content.tip: 'PJ' (Pessoa Jurídica) roughly maps to 'independent contractor' or 'freelancer' in English-speaking markets.

content.subtitle: Giving and Receiving Feedback
content.explanation: Constructive feedback in English workplaces is often 'sandwiched' — positive, then improvement, then encouragement.
examples: I really liked how you handled the client call — very clear and confident.
One thing to work on: try to summarize next steps at the end of each meeting.
Overall, great progress this sprint — keep it up!
Thanks for the feedback, I'll definitely work on that.
Could you give me an example of what you mean?
content.tip: Use 'I feel...' or 'I noticed...' rather than 'you always...' to keep feedback constructive, not accusatory.

sections.title: Culture & Social Understanding
sections.description: Communication styles, etiquette, humor, and everyday culture in English-speaking countries

content.subtitle: Direct vs Indirect Communication
content.explanation: English-speaking business cultures (especially US/UK) tend to value directness, but they soften statements with politeness markers rather than being blunt.
examples: Direct but polite: 'I don't think this approach will work. Could we consider an alternative?'
Too indirect (avoid): 'Maybe, perhaps, possibly it could be an idea to think about changing it a little...'
Disagreeing politely: 'I see your point, but I'd like to offer a different perspective.'
Softening a request: 'Would it be possible to get this by Thursday?' instead of 'Give me this by Thursday.'
content.tip: Brazilian and French communication often uses more context and warmth before the main point — in English business settings, get to the point sooner, but stay warm.

content.subtitle: Small Talk & Icebreakers
content.explanation: Small talk is a social ritual in English-speaking cultures — it builds rapport before business or deeper conversation.
examples: 'How was your weekend?' — a very common opener at work on Mondays.
'Did you catch the game last night?' — sports as a safe, common topic.
'This weather, huh?' — commenting on weather is a classic, safe icebreaker in the UK.
'How's it going?' 'Not bad, you?' — a casual greeting exchange, not a real question about your life.
content.tip: Avoid asking about salary, age, weight, or religion in small talk — these are considered too personal in most English-speaking cultures.

content.subtitle: Politeness Strategies & Hedging
content.explanation: Native speakers often 'hedge' statements to sound less forceful, especially in professional contexts.
examples: 'I was just wondering if maybe we could reschedule...' (soft request)
'It might be worth considering...' (soft suggestion)
'I could be wrong, but I think the deadline moved.' (soft opinion)
'Sorry to bother you, but could I ask a quick question?' (polite interruption)
content.tip: Hedging isn't weakness — it's a social skill. Overusing very direct commands can come across as rude in English, even if grammatically correct.

content.subtitle: Major Holidays in English-Speaking Countries
content.explanation: Knowing key holidays helps you understand context in conversations, emails ('Happy Thanksgiving!'), and scheduling.
examples: Thanksgiving (USA, 4th Thursday of November): family dinner with turkey, giving thanks.
Independence Day (USA, July 4th): fireworks, barbecues, national pride.
Boxing Day (UK/Canada, December 26th): a shopping and relaxation day after Christmas.
Halloween (Oct 31st): costumes, trick-or-treating, pumpkin carving — widely celebrated in the US, UK, and Canada.
St. Patrick's Day (March 17th): Irish culture celebration, popular worldwide.
content.tip: In work emails around these dates, it's common to write 'Happy Thanksgiving!' or 'Have a great long weekend!'

content.subtitle: Food & Dining Culture
content.explanation: Dining customs vary — understanding them avoids awkward moments while traveling or working abroad.
examples: In the US, it's common to ask for a 'to-go box' (doggy bag) to take leftovers home.
In the UK, tea is often offered as a gesture of hospitality: 'Would you like a cup of tea?'
Splitting the bill ('going Dutch') is very common among friends in the US, UK, and Canada.
'BYOB' (Bring Your Own Bottle) parties are common and expected at some casual gatherings.
content.tip: Tipping culture differs sharply: in the US, 15-20% is expected at restaurants; in the UK it's optional (usually 10%); it's not customary in many other countries.

content.subtitle: Tipping, Manners & Social Norms
content.explanation: Small social rules can make a big impression when studying, traveling, or working internationally.
examples: Holding the door open for the person behind you is standard courtesy in the US and UK.
Queuing (standing in line) is taken very seriously in the UK — never cut the line.
In business meetings, arriving exactly on time (not early, not late) is considered professional in the US.
A firm handshake and eye contact are typically expected in professional introductions.
content.tip: When in doubt, observe before acting — cultural norms vary even within English-speaking countries (US, UK, Canada, Australia, Ireland).

content.subtitle: Idioms Rooted in History & Culture
content.explanation: Many idioms come from historical or cultural references — knowing the story helps you remember the meaning.
examples: 'Bite the bullet' — to do something difficult or unpleasant (from soldiers biting a bullet during surgery, before anesthesia).
'Spill the beans' — to reveal a secret (from ancient voting systems using beans).
'Break the ice' — to ease tension in a social situation (from ships literally breaking ice to open trade routes).
'Once in a blue moon' — something that happens very rarely.
content.tip: You don't need to know the history to use idioms correctly, but it makes them much easier to remember.

content.subtitle: British vs American English Differences
content.explanation: Vocabulary, spelling, and even meaning can shift between British and American English — important for study or work abroad.
examples: Apartment (US) vs Flat (UK)
Elevator (US) vs Lift (UK)
Vacation (US) vs Holiday (UK)
Color (US spelling) vs Colour (UK spelling)
'Football' means soccer in the UK, but American football in the US.
content.tip: Pick one variety (US or UK) for formal writing like a CV or academic essay, and stay consistent throughout the document.

content.subtitle: Understanding Humor & Sarcasm
content.explanation: British humor especially relies heavily on sarcasm and understatement, which can confuse non-native speakers.
examples: 'Oh brilliant, another Monday.' (sarcastic — actually means the opposite)
Understatement: after a disaster, saying 'That could have gone better.'
Self-deprecating humor is common and seen as endearing, not weak, in British culture.
Tone of voice and context matter more than the literal words — sarcasm is often signaled by a flat or exaggerated tone.
content.tip: If you're unsure whether someone is joking, it's okay to smile and ask: 'Wait, are you being serious?'

sections.title: Study Abroad & Academic Life
sections.description: Applications, scholarships, visas, and university vocabulary for studying internationally

content.subtitle: Application Vocabulary
content.explanation: Understanding key admissions terms helps you navigate university websites and application portals confidently.
examples: Undergraduate: a bachelor's degree program (first university degree).
Graduate / Postgraduate: master's or doctoral studies after a bachelor's degree.
Transcript: an official record of your grades and courses.
Deadline: the final date to submit an application — 'The deadline is January 15th.'
Rolling admissions: applications are reviewed as they arrive, not all at once.
content.tip: Always check whether a deadline is by 11:59 PM in the university's local time zone — many students miss deadlines because of time zone confusion.

content.subtitle: Personal Statement / Motivation Letter
content.explanation: This is your chance to explain, in your own voice, why you're a strong candidate — beyond grades and test scores.
examples: 'My interest in computer science began when I built my first website at 16.'
'Studying at [University] would allow me to combine my technical background with your renowned research in AI.'
'I am particularly drawn to this program because of its emphasis on practical, industry-focused learning.'
'This opportunity would be a pivotal step in achieving my long-term goal of leading technology projects that create real social impact.'
content.tip: Avoid generic statements like 'I've always wanted to study abroad.' Be specific about the program, professors, or research that attracted you.

content.subtitle: Letters of Recommendation
content.explanation: Recommendation letters are usually written by professors or supervisors — but you often need to request them politely and provide context.
examples: 'I was wondering if you would be willing to write a letter of recommendation for my master's application.'
'I've attached my resume and a summary of the program to make the process easier.'
'The deadline for submission is March 1st — please let me know if that timeline works for you.'
'Thank you so much for considering this — I really valued your guidance during the Data Structures course.'
content.tip: Ask at least 3-4 weeks before the deadline, and always thank the person afterward, regardless of the outcome.

content.subtitle: Scholarship & Funding Vocabulary
content.explanation: Financial vocabulary is essential to understand what a scholarship actually covers.
examples: Tuition fee: the cost of the academic program itself.
Full ride: a scholarship covering all costs (tuition, housing, sometimes living expenses).
Stipend: a regular payment to cover living expenses, often for research or teaching assistants.
Need-based aid: financial support based on your financial situation.
Merit-based scholarship: awarded based on academic or other achievements, not financial need.
content.tip: Always read the fine print: some scholarships only cover tuition and not housing, insurance, or flights.

content.subtitle: Student Visa Process
content.explanation: Visa vocabulary and processes vary by country, but certain terms are nearly universal.
examples: 'I need to provide proof of enrollment before applying for my student visa.'
'Financial statement: bank documents proving you can support yourself during your studies.'
'The embassy requires an in-person interview as part of the visa process.'
'My visa allows me to work part-time up to 20 hours per week during term time.'
content.tip: Start the visa process early — processing times can take weeks or months depending on the country and season.

content.subtitle: Budgeting & Cost of Living Abroad
content.explanation: Being able to discuss your budget in English helps with housing searches, roommate arrangements, and part-time work.
examples: 'My monthly budget covers rent, groceries, and transportation, with a small amount left for savings.'
'Is the rent inclusive of utilities, or do I need to pay them separately?'
'I'm looking for a shared apartment to reduce living costs.'
'Do you know if there's a student discount for public transportation?'
content.tip: Ask locals or student groups about 'hidden costs' like deposits, agency fees, or mandatory health insurance before committing to housing.

content.subtitle: Lectures, Seminars & Assignments
content.explanation: University life has its own vocabulary that differs from general classroom English.
examples: Lecture: a large class where a professor presents information, usually with little discussion.
Seminar: a smaller, discussion-based class where participation is expected.
Office hours: scheduled time when professors are available for questions — 'I'll stop by during office hours.'
Syllabus: the document outlining course content, readings, and grading.
'The assignment is due by midnight on Friday, submitted through the online portal.'
content.tip: Ask professors 'Could you clarify the expectations for this assignment?' if instructions are unclear — this is completely normal and expected.

content.subtitle: Academic Integrity & Citations
content.explanation: Understanding academic honesty rules is critical — norms can be stricter abroad than what you're used to.
examples: Plagiarism: presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own — taken very seriously abroad.
Citation: giving credit to a source, e.g., '(Smith, 2021)' in APA style.
'Please make sure to properly cite all sources used in your essay.'
'Group work is allowed for this project, but the final write-up must be done individually.'
content.tip: When in doubt about what counts as plagiarism, ask your professor or check your university's academic integrity policy — penalties can be severe.

content.subtitle: Making Friends & Student Housing
content.explanation: Social vocabulary helps you settle in faster, both academically and personally.
examples: 'Do you want to grab a coffee sometime this week?' — a common way to build friendships.
Dorm / Halls of residence: on-campus student housing.
'I'm looking for a roommate to split rent for a two-bedroom apartment near campus.'
Freshers' Week (UK) / Welcome Week (US): the first week of university, full of social events for new students.
'There's an international students' club that organizes weekly meetups — you should join!'
content.tip: Joining clubs and student associations is one of the fastest ways to build a social network and practice English naturally.
